versions.name: 1.0 Trust & Monetization Fixes
versions.summary: Fix the highest-severity problems: make paywall boundaries explicit, guarantee free-trial and billing integrity, repair the free-tier ad experience, preserve a meaningful free workout path, and make support responsive.
versions.rationale: Findings 1, 2, 3, 5, and 8 show that surprise charges, unlabeled paywalls, forced 90-second ads, and unreachable support are the most severe and trust-damaging themes. These issues also drive the polarizing subscription-value split, so they must be addressed before content or personalization work can land effectively.

versions.name: 2.0 Content, Personalization & Opportunities
versions.summary: Resolve the polarizing workout-content split, honor user goals and restrictions, and ship concrete requests: Apple Watch sync, adaptive programs, and workout control options. Rebuild subscription value messaging around outcomes and flexibility.
versions.rationale: Findings 4, 6, and 7 show that after trust issues are fixed, the next lever is making the app feel tailored, safe, and genuinely useful. These changes directly address the 'AI slop' vs 'love the variety' split and the unmet needs expressed by older, pregnant, or injury-avoiding users.

planningFactors.rationale: Finding 1 shows this is a frequent reason for churn and trust loss; finding 8 highlights the same feature is praised by subscribers, so transparency is the bridge between the two sides. Scope is medium because it touches UI labels, content metadata, and onboarding flow.

Finding 2 and several supporting reviews in finding 8 describe real money being taken without clear consent, which is the highest-severity trust issue. Scope is medium because it involves StoreKit purchase flows, subscription management UI, and notification scheduling.

Finding 3 shows broken ad UX can hijack the app entirely, and finding 1 shows it pushes formerly loyal users away. Scope is medium because it requires ad SDK configuration, close-control handling, and a no-redirect safeguard.

Finding 1 shows the removal of formerly free workouts is the core churn driver; finding 5 shows daily short workouts are the most-loved habit; finding 8 shows some users still find the subscription worth it. This requirement restores the free path without eliminating the paid value proposition.

Finding 6 documents ignored preferences and exclusionary content, which damages trust and can pose safety risks. Finding 4 shows content quality is polarizing, so plan generation must at least respect the user's stated constraints. Scope is large because it requires tagging, plan generation logic, and onboarding changes.

Finding 4 shows the same workout library is beloved by some and criticized by others; finding 7 and finding 5 provide concrete directions for demos and short sessions. Scope is large because it involves content production, demo assets, and plan-generation rotation rules.
Finding 7 contains the direct Apple Watch request, and finding 4 shows a reviewer wishing the app connected to a watch. Scope is medium because HealthKit integration and watch app work are moderate.

Finding 6 documents the pregnancy-safety complaint and forced-goal problem; finding 7 contains the older-adult program request; finding 4 shows no-floor workouts are already appreciated. Scope is medium because it adds new content and filtering logic.

Finding 7 includes the voice-prompt and shorter-ad requests; finding 6 includes the no-jump and longer-interval requests; finding 5 shows the daily short workout is a loved habit that these controls protect. Scope is medium because it touches settings, workout player, and plan substitution.

Finding 8 explicitly shows the same subscription is seen as transformative by some and as a paywall by others; finding 1 shows former free access is the main complaint; finding 2 shows billing surprises amplify the negative view. This requirement directly addresses the polarizing value perception and depends on transparent labeling first.

Finding 2 shows support failures compound billing and login issues, turning a bad moment into a permanent trust loss. Implementable independently as a support workflow and form fix, so it belongs in the trust-focused first version.
